summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 3/8 of 24) is a two-step operator procedure for 8-9 year olds: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part, then multiply that part by the numerator. Children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence, grounding it in the meaning of numerator and denominator, and translating worded problems into that structure. Make the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them.
misconceptions: Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator (3/8 of 24 read as 24 ÷ 3)
Stops after one step — finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and gives that as the answer without multiplying by the numerator
Multiplies the whole by the numerator (24 × 3) giving an answer larger than the whole
Multiplies numerator and denominator into the whole in the wrong order or muddles which is which under worded-problem load

activities.title: The fraction-of machine: divide to build parts, then take them
steps: Set up the problem '3/8 of 24 sweets': start with 24 sweets to share.
Split the 24 sweets into equal groups, where the number of groups is fixed by the denominator (8 groups of 3).
Now take the numerator's worth of those groups: take 3 of the 8 groups and count the total (9).
Record the two steps in writing alongside the action: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9.
Repeat with new fractions and new contexts (e.g. 3/5 of 20 pounds, 2/3 of 18 people) so the structure, not one phrasing, is practised.
activities.insight: The procedure is two distinct actions with two distinct results: dividing by the denominator builds the equal parts, and multiplying by the numerator (selecting that many groups) takes them. Children can self-check which number divides (how many equal shares) and which multiplies (how many shares to take).

activities.title: Isolate the new step: from unit fraction to non-unit fraction
steps: First confirm the unit fraction on secure ground: find 1/8 of 24 (= 3).
Then isolate the new step: 'That is one group. For 3/8, how many groups do we take?' Take 3 groups to get 9.
Try the same whole with a different numerator: 5/8 of 24 re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (= 15); notice you do NOT re-divide.
Explain in your own words why the denominator divides and the numerator multiplies.
activities.insight: The division step is shared across all eighths of 24; only the numerator (how many groups to take) changes. This separates the secure prior skill from the genuinely new multiply-by-numerator step.

activities.title: Bar models and arrays: making divide-then-multiply visible
steps: Draw the whole as a bar labelled 24; partition it into the denominator's number of equal parts (8 parts), label one part (3).
Shade the numerator's number of parts (3 parts) and read off the shaded total (9).
Build the same with counters: arrange 24 counters as 8 groups of 3, then ring 3 groups.
Use a double number line: amount (0 to 24) on top and fraction (0 to 1, marked in eighths) on the bottom, so 1/8 lines up with 3 and 8/8 lines up with 24. Mark one part, then step along to 3/8 (9).
activities.insight: The model makes the divide-then-multiply structure visible: partitioning is the division, shading/selecting is the multiplication. Reading the total off the model catches the divide-by-numerator error (wrong number of parts) and the multiply-the-whole error (answer must fit inside the bar).

activities.title: Varied worded problems and plausibility checking
steps: Solve worded problems across contexts: sweets (A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red - how many red?), money (3/5 of 20 pounds), measures (cm), and sets of people (2/3 of 18).
For each, write the two lines of working and name which number divides and which multiplies.
Before accepting an answer, run the plausibility check: a proper fraction of an amount must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24 is reasonable; 72 is not).
Optionally talk a problem through aloud with a partner or in-role 'shopkeeper' who poses 'fraction of my stock' problems, explaining each step.
activities.insight: Translating varied language into the same divide-then-multiply structure prevents pattern-matching one phrasing, and the plausibility check guards against multiply-the-whole errors.

checkQuestion: Here are 24 counters. Find 3/8 of them. Do it however you like, and I'll watch — you don't need to tell me the rule.
checkAnswer: 9. The child splits the 24 into 8 equal groups (24 ÷ 8 = 3 in each), then takes 3 of those groups (3 × 3 = 9).
